findings.element: .b-plan and .b-stick — the two scrolling panes of the owner's fixed desk frame, 1024 and above
findings.problem: The fixed frame is a real decision, but neither pane's fold is drawn. Measured at 1440x960: .b-plan is 664px tall around 1727px of plan, so 1063px (62%) is below the fold and only two of the seven moments are on screen, while 337px of the 664px rail pane beside it (51%) is blank. Computed maskImage is none on both panes, ::before and ::after are none, and no scrollbar gutter is reserved — the fold is a hard cut through whatever happens to be at that y. Sampling ten common window sizes: at 1366x768 (the commonest laptop there is) the cut halves the title 'Send the invitations' and its count '23'; at 1280x800 it halves 'Sat 8 Aug'; at 1024x700 and 1920x1080 it halves an 'Edit' control that is still clickable at half height. In each case the sliced half-line sits 4-20px above the page's closing footer rule, so it reads as broken rendering rather than as 'there is more below'. The top edge is the same once scrolled (owner-undone): the rail is cut mid-stroke and the DAYS AWAY head and the 'Today, 16 July' origin have silently gone with no sign they exist. This is the lessons library's guillotine, newly created by round 8's frame.
findings.fix: In b.css, at the >=1024 rule, give .b-plan and .b-stick: --fadeTop:0px; --fadeBot:0px; mask-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, transparent 0, #000 var(--fadeTop), #000 calc(100% - var(--fadeBot)), transparent 100%); and -webkit-mask-image the same. Set both to 40px only via [data-fade~="top"] / [data-fade~="bottom"]. In render-b.js, on each pane's scroll (rAF-throttled) and after every repaint and resize, measure and write data-fade: 'top' when scrollTop > 2, 'bottom' when scrollHeight - clientHeight - scrollTop > 2, both when both, and remove the attribute when nothing is hidden — measured after layout, so a fade always means something is actually hidden.

findings.element: .b-gapNote inside the sticky .b-stick, state=desk at 1024 and above
findings.problem: The mechanism that keeps the pinned column honest is built, but it is wired only to the owner's pane scroller. Driven: in owner-flight at 1440, scrolling .b-plan by 1200px changes the pinned line from 'Nothing is planned until 1 August.' to '19 September · 65 days away'. In the received desk state the same column is position:sticky (confirmed at 1152 and 1440) and therefore never leaves the audience's screen — but the window is the scroller there, and scrolling it 1200px leaves the line still reading 'Nothing is planned until 1 August.' with rows 44 / 51 / 65 / 79 (29 August to 3 October) as the only things beside it. The one sentence that is always on a guest's screen is the only thing on the page contradicting what is next to it, and this is the surface a venue or a parent actually receives.
findings.fix: In render-b.js, the readout updater is bound to the .b-plan scroll event. Extract it to a function taking a scroller argument, and in the received desk layout (where .b-stick is sticky and .b-plan is not a scroller) bind the same function to the window scroll, rAF-throttled, using the same accessor and the same rule already asserted for the owner — the nearest item whose top has passed the top of the viewport, and back to the gap note when the gap is on screen.

findings.element: .b-who and .b-measureHead at 1024 and above, and on the printed A4 sheet
findings.problem: The two columns start at exactly the same y — 230.9 at 1440, 108.4 on the sheet — but .b-measureHead carries margin-top:20px, inherited from the stacked layout below 1024 where it is the gap between the horizon and the plan. So the page's two column labels, both Geist Mono uppercase micro-labels in the same register, miss each other by 20px: MARA & FINN at 230.9, DAYS AWAY at 250.9. Nothing else in either column sits at that height, so the offset has nothing to justify it and reads as a near-miss rather than a stagger — the boxes align mathematically and the ink does not. It prints the same way on the keepsake.
findings.fix: In b.css, inside the >=1024 two-pane rule (and the print rule), add `.b-plan > .b-measureHead { margin-top: 0 }` so the two labels' boxes and baselines coincide within 1px; leave the 20px in place below 1024 where it is doing real work. If the stagger is wanted, take it to 40px instead so it reads as a decision, but do not leave it at one line height.

findings.problem: The white message plate is 560px wide at 768, 1152 and 1440 while everything it holds — .b-bubble and .b-unfurl — is capped at max-width:300px. That gives it 16px of white to the left of the message, 244px to the right, against 28px top and bottom: three sides padded on the scale, one side fifteen times it. The same component in the publish state renders correctly, 320px of plate around a 286px card. Because the plate is pure white on ink it is the brightest rectangle in the whole fourteen-state set, and 44% of it is empty on the one state whose only job is to show what the audience sees before they open the link.
findings.fix: In b.css, for the unfurl state's .b-chat set `width: fit-content; max-width: 332px; margin-inline: auto` (16 + 300 + 16) so the plate closes on the same 16px margin it opens on at every width; keep the 390 case unchanged, where it already fits. Alternatively raise .b-bubble and .b-unfurl to max-width:528px so they fill the existing 560 plate — but the first is the smaller change and keeps the card at the size a real thread draws it.

biggestWin: The horizon and the measure are one composition, not two panels sharing a page. The count is a true focal object — 96/148px, its numeral pulled 7.4px left of the column so the 7 reads flush — and the eye lands on it first, then falls to the date, then across to the rail, which is exactly the right order for a page whose subject is a distance. Under it the craft is real and consistent: the whole horizon block runs on a 4px scale (20/12/4/28/8/16), the phone cards in the ended, loading and morning states all close on the same 28px margin they open on, the A4 keepsake is a properly gridded sheet with 56px margins and the same optical overhang on its numeral, and the two-pane desk frame keeps its own promise — the horizon holds still, focus is scrolled into the visible part of the pane on every tab, and the pinned readout follows the plan. Fourteen states are composed rather than defaulted. What stands between this and 9.5 is not structure and not a different decision: it is the fold. Both scrolling panes were given a frame in round 8 and never given an edge, and one wired-up scroll listener is missing from the surface the audience actually receives. That is polish plus one small build — a day's work, not a rethink.
